draft.title: Shelter as a right
card: International law treats adequate housing as a human right. The International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) recognises the right to an adequate standard of living, which includes housing.
Adequate housing means more than a roof. It includes secure tenure, affordability, safe and liveable conditions, and access to services.
Australia has ratified the ICESCR, so it has agreed to work towards this right. A treaty does not become part of Australian law until Parliament passes a law that includes it.
Parliament has not passed a law that gives people a right to housing, and the Australian Constitution does not protect one. A person cannot go to court and claim a home as a legal right.
draft.remember: Housing is a right in international law, but Australian law does not give a right to a home.

a.q: Which statement best describes the right to housing in Australia?
opts: It is set out in a treaty but not in Australian law
It is protected by the Australian Constitution
Australian courts can enforce it as a legal right
It is not recognised in international law
a.why: Australia has ratified the ICESCR, but Parliament has not passed a law giving a right to housing. The Constitution option is wrong because it does not protect this right.
a.clue: Think about what must happen before a treaty becomes Australian law.

b.q: Sam has been on a waiting list for housing in Sydney for years. He says Australia has ratified a treaty on housing, so a court must give him a home. Why is he wrong?
opts: Parliament has not made a law giving a right to housing
Australia has not signed any treaty that mentions housing
A treaty only applies to people who own their own homes
Courts can only order housing for people who rent
b.why: A ratified treaty does not become Australian law until Parliament passes a law that includes it. No such law gives a right to housing, so a court has nothing to enforce. Saying Australia has not signed a treaty is wrong, because it has ratified the ICESCR.
b.clue: Ratifying a treaty is not the same as making it law.

a.best: It is set out in a treaty but not in Australian law

b.best: Parliament has not made a law giving a right to housing
